title: Building trust in AI agents: A production-ready evaluation framework with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: The North Star Every organization racing to deploy AI agents faces the same reckoning: an agent that demos beautifully can quietly degrade in production, and by the time a human notices, the trust is already broken. Where traditional software fails loudly, agents fail softly. They return an answer that looks confident, reads fluently, and is wrong. When that answer drives a real business decision, the cost is not a broken feature. It’s a broken relationship with the user. That’s the quality problem at its core. The challenge is therefore not building agents that work once, but proving they keep working, at scale, across every sub-agent, every workflow, and every release. The teams that win the agent era will be the ones who treat quality not as a final QA step but as the operating system of the agent itself: continuously measured, automatically defended, and improved with every interaction. In this post, we show how we built a continuous quality loop for production-ready agentic solutions at scale using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Business problem The solution uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and other AWS services for internal use, so sellers and sales leaders can ask business questions in plain English from Amazon Quick. Behind that single experience, several specialized sub-agents work together: the Performance Insights Agent for territory-scoped revenue and performance, the Customer Insights Agent for customer intelligence, the Data Insights Agent for text-to-SQL over foundational datasets, and direct dashboard access. Answers are scoped to each user’s territory and role-level security. Field teams use these answers to assist in planning account strategy, prepare for customer meetings, so the numbers must be right. The most damaging failure is not a crash. It’s a fluent, confident answer that is quietly wrong. Before launch, when we evaluated the Customer Insights Agent, we found exactly that: It reported $410.08 of a customer’s three-month revenue on a service as “$410.08 Million.” It reported Sales Revenue labeled as Sales Revenue excluding Adjustments. It offered an Annual Recurring Revenue estimate that appeared nowhere in the data. It presented its own calculations as sourced facts. Through the different runs, monitoring stayed green. It told us the system had responded, not whether the answer was right. Had these errors shipped uncaught, the field would have paid for them. A seller who repeats an inflated figure can lose credibility with the customer. This is exactly why we caught it before launch. The risk doesn’t end at launch: it grows with every new agent and every change to data, prompts, code, or models. It also grows without any release, because upstream pipelines refresh the data every week. Coordinated releases introduce a related risk: when a data change, a tool change, and a paired prompt update are meant to ship together but land apart, the system runs mismatched until all changes catch up. In one pre-production test, that mismatch window by itself dropped the pass rate from 78 percent to 38 percent. To catch failures like these, before every release and continuously in production, we need a framework that can show whether answers are grounded and correct, and trace each failure back to its root cause in the data, the prompt, or the agent’s code. At AWS, the Sales, Marketing, and Global Services (SMGS) Operations team developed a production multi-agent system serving AWS Field Sales worldwide. It serves two distinct audiences. For field sales teams, it replaces hours of manual data analysis with on-demand, conversational intelligence, helping sellers understand the health of their business, surface risks and opportunities, and take action faster. For leadership, it powers business management cadences including Weekly Business Reviews (WBRs), surfacing the signals that matter across the portfolio without requiring manual report preparation. title: Introducing Reflection Beam: an open-weight model for agentic coding on AWS
abstract: Reflection AI introduced Beam, an open-weight model for agentic coding and long-horizon tasks such as maintaining code, using tools, interpreting results, and completing multi-step workflows. The open-weight release gives developers and researchers control over the runtime, deployment environment, and customization process. In this post, we explain Reflection’s vision and show how you can deploy Beam on AWS. Start with an Amazon SageMaker JumpStart real-time endpoint for a fully managed path. When you need Kubernetes-native control over distributed GPU infrastructure, use Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference with JumpStart, SGLang, or vLLM. We also explain how Beam’s 501 billion total parameters shape checkpoint storage, weight memory, sharding, and parallelism, while its 23 billion active parameters influence per-token compute. At launch, Beam is available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart in US East (N. Virginia) and US East (Ohio). Reflection’s vision for open intelligence Reflection’s mission is to make intelligence open and accessible to all through open model weights, published research, and open source software. Its full AI stack spans models, core software, production infrastructure, and applications. Beam brings this approach to developers building software engineering and agentic systems. About Reflection Beam Beam is a sparse mixture-of-experts model for resolving software issues, modifying code, calling tools, and acting on intermediate results. It has 501 billion total parameters and 23 billion active parameters, and Reflection reports an effective context length of 1 million tokens. Reflection releases Beam’s weights through Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license. Beam 1.0 is available in BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 checkpoint variants. These formats provide different memory footprints and hardware compatibility. You can deploy the model with the AWS managed JumpStart container configuration or inspect and customize the model with SGLang or vLLM in your AWS environment. Understand the deployment architecture Choose the serving path that meets your control and scaling requirements. Start with a SageMaker JumpStart real-time endpoint when you want an AWS managed model package, endpoint, and invocation API without operating Kubernetes. Use JumpStart on HyperPod Inference when you want the AWS managed container and model configuration on a HyperPod cluster orchestrated by Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). Use SGLang or vLLM on HyperPod Inference when you need to control the serving image, runtime arguments, quantization, or distributed execution. Size the deployment for checkpoint storage, weight memory, KV cache, context length, batching, runtime overhead, and the supported parallelism. Define the expected concurrency and latency targets, then configure replicas, caching, routing, and autoscaling from measured workload behavior. The JumpStart real-time path packages the model, container, and endpoint behind a managed deployment workflow. The HyperPod path exposes the cluster and serving runtime so that you can control distributed execution, caching, routing, and scaling. Beam can be sourced through SageMaker JumpStart, Hugging Face Hub, or an optional Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) mirror. The distributed workers use the AWS managed JumpStart container or a custom SGLang or vLLM runtime. title: Ontology-Driven Observability: Building an End-to-End Knowledge Graph at Netflix Scale
abstract: Prasanna Vijayanathan , Renzo Sanchez-Silva When Jake Paul and Mike Tyson stepped into the ring in November 2024, we delivered the fight to roughly 65 million concurrent streams. On an ordinary day our infrastructure takes in more than 2 billion requests and handles upwards of 38 million real-time logging events every second. At that scale, the whole picture doesn’t fit into a single engineering team’s head or onto a single dashboard. With more Live content, Podcasts and real-time streams, our need to understand and update our systems as quickly as possible becomes imperative to provide a good user experience. Understanding the system at this scale and within the time constraints we have, often becomes a daunting exercise in finding a needle in a haystack, in a dark jungle, blindfolded. This post is about that search for the needle. The Four hours before a fix Consider a regression of the kind we see in a given week. The home screen where you see the list of lists of movies, starts taking about 1.5 seconds longer to render. An alert fires. And then we go looking for what caused this issue and how do we fix it? As it so happens, a regression on the application could be related to anywhere in the system — a client app regression from a new version deployment or A/B test rollout, a load shedding in the infrastructure, a GraphQL query responding with bad data because of a service rollout 6 hops downstream, are all suspects at this point. So, answering “what caused the issue?” needs insights from across the system, and this involves combing through layers of data in a meticulous manner. The MELT Layer “What caused the issue?” Metrics, events, logs and traces, or MELT, in the industry’s shorthand, are the right raw materials for such an investigation, and each of them answers roughly a quarter of the question. We collect observability data across these four pillars, unified into a single observability data layer. This lets us observe our systems in real time, across what our users are experiencing, how our applications are doing and what our backend infrastructure and services are processing and responding to. MELT — Metrics, Events, Logs and Traces, and how they are captured across the system. The investigation that follows may look like this in each layer: What each layer of MELT tells us and what it leaves out The timeline of an investigation So how long does it take to investigate an issue, figure out the root cause and fix it, so our users stop running into this issue again? A timeline of an investigation: ~4 hours In our chosen example, four hours. Very little of it went into computing anything difficult. Most of it went into reconstructing relationships that our observability systems already knew but we had never written down anywhere a human or machine could simply read and discover. The disagreement underneath The instinct here could have been, around 2023, to reach for more data or better dashboards, and while both help at the margins, neither addresses what makes these investigations slow. It’s 2026 now, so we might say, “hey, agents”, but without the right context delivered to the agents, AI systems hallucinate, and especially when teams are on-call and need a fix “now”, we cannot let inaccurate agentic analysis lead us down the wrong path. We need the right needle, not any needle. Each of our systems is internally coherent and externally isolated. Atlas , our telemetry platform, knows applications and their time series. Radar, our alerting system, knows thresholds and firing history. incident.io knows severities and responders. PagerDuty knows rotations. Spinnaker knows what shipped and when. And our Slack history knows, in a form no query engine can reach, which engineer solved something very similar last quarter and what they found. This Week in AI: Expanding the Possibilities
abstract: New AI tools are making business data easier to explore. They’re also giving researchers new ways to study disease outbreaks and physical systems. On the latest episode of This Week in AI , we examined developments from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Mistral, new research on the economics of robotics, and how scientists are using AI to tackle difficult problems. New AI tools put more capabilities directly in users’ hands OpenAI’s new Intelligent UI feature lets ChatGPT generate visual explanations and interactive tools directly in conversations. With the launch of MCP Events , supported connected applications can notify ChatGPT when something happens. If a user has asked ChatGPT to watch for that event, it can follow their instructions and take requested actions without waiting for another prompt. Anthropic’s Claude Dashboards brings natural-language queries and interactive visualizations to company data. Claude Motion adds another visual capability, turning reports and charts into editable animations. Self-service dashboards can create a range of problems though. For example, employees may reference incomplete data or apply different definitions to the same metric, then share their results as authoritative. As more employees take on exploratory analysis, BI teams will need to expand their role by maintaining reliable data and shared definitions, setting clear governance and access rules, helping employees interpret results responsibly, and monitoring how dashboards are used. Beyond the big two, Mistral previewed Large 4 , a trillion-parameter open-weight model designed for coding, agents, and multimodal tasks. The company plans to release the model’s weights soon, giving developers access to another large model for building and running AI applications. As AI agents gain access to more applications and company data, organizations will need clearer rules about what those agents can access and when humans should intervene. Recent internal tests at Anthropic showed how difficult it can be to control agents once they have access to external systems. The company reported cases of Claude circumventing restrictions, including copying server files and submitting fabricated forms, and subsequently restricted live internet access in internal tests until they’re better able to monitor their systems. OpenAI also announced plans for text watermarking in the EU , though editing and short passages can make watermarks difficult to detect reliably. Robotics research puts automation forecasts in perspective A new Anthropic study offered a useful counterpoint to predictions of widespread job displacement. Researchers found that existing robots could perform tasks accounting for roughly 34% of US work hours, but doing so would be cost competitive for just 0.3% of work hours. Most of these tasks take place in structured environments such as factories, where robots can operate more reliably than in unpredictable settings. When researchers combined the potential exposure of cognitive work to language models with physical work exposed to robotics, the share of work hours potentially affected reached 81%. For employers and policymakers, exposure figures help identify which tasks could change, but they don’t predict how many jobs automation will eliminate. Deployment costs, working conditions, and the need for human judgment will influence how quickly employers adopt these technologies . As we discussed during the audience Q&A, jobs are already changing, particularly in technical fields, even without evidence of massive displacement. For now, employers may get more value from helping workers develop new skills than from planning around speculative job-loss forecasts. AI is opening new avenues for scientific research AI is helping researchers tackle problems in mathematics, biology, space, and public health. title: Code Review After Code Gets Cheap
abstract: In my previous article , I argued that agentic development needs enough specification to make correctness checkable. A quick prompt can get implementation started quickly, but someone still has to decide whether the result does what we wanted. I left a fairly practical question unanswered, though. Once the agent has written the code, how should we review it? You can give an agent a clear task and get back a serious implementation with tests. The build passes and the code looks reasonable. Now somebody has to approve the pull request, and that person has roughly the same amount of time they had before code generation became cheap. Reading every changed line is one way to approach this. But if each increase in generated code requires a similar increase in human inspection, review will keep limiting how many changes we can accept. We need a way to decide where that inspection is worth the effort. My approach is to make evidence a condition of accepting agent-generated code. Agree on the intended behavior and the expected blast radius before implementation starts. Then use the evidence to check for drift and decide which parts of the code need direct inspection. So far, that may sound like test-driven development. But what happens when every test passes and the agent has added behavior nobody asked for? A small diff can have a large blast radius Let’s use a small fictional example. Suppose we are adding an approval step to a refund service. Refunds above €100 require approval from an authorized employee before the service sends the payment request. Exactly €100 does not require this additional approval. The existing rules about who can request a refund continue to apply. An agent implements the approval step and adds tests. While updating the payment integration, it also adds retries after a timeout. That seems reasonable enough. Network calls fail, and retrying them is a familiar engineering practice. But a timeout leaves us with another question. The provider may have issued the refund before its response was lost. Sending the request again could issue a second refund. Whether that can happen depends on how the provider handles repeated requests and how our code uses that behavior. The approval feature may be correct while the added retry introduces a separate problem. I can see a human review focusing only on the requested feature and easily missing the new decision about payment behavior. By blast radius, I mean how far the effects of a mistake can spread. If the agent puts the retry in a shared payment client, it may affect every refund, including those below the approval threshold. The change now reaches beyond the feature we asked for. Counting the changed lines won’t tell us that. Treat blast radius as a review criterion on its own. Establish which operations a change is allowed to affect, then check whether the implementation stays within that boundary. Also consider how hard a mistake would be to undo. Deploying the previous version won’t recover money that has already been refunded twice. Look for drift in both directions This is the kind of drift I want a review process to expose. We need to check that the requested behavior exists and examine additional behavior that could affect the system. There is an established name for following these relationships in both directions: bidirectional traceability. NASA’s software engineering guidance describes tracing requirements through implementation and verification, including finding functionality that has no parent requirement. I think that the basic idea translates quite well to an ordinary pull request. For each important requirement, we should be able to find the implementation and the checks that support it. Looking back from the implementation, we should be able to explain why a change to behavior belongs in this pull request. An extra private method will usually need little discussion. title: This implant can restore sight for patients with macular degeneration
abstract: More than 5 million people around the world with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) experience atrophy in their retinas. And until now, no treatment could restore their vision. The PRIMA system, which was approved in Europe in July and is awaiting FDA clearance in the US, changes that. It combines a retinal implant with camera-­equipped eyeglasses to improve sight in patients who develop a blind spot in the middle of their vision due to advanced AMD. After training sessions, more than 80% of recipients were able to read, do crosswords, and use their phones. The retina processes light in three layers of cells: Photoreceptors convert light into electricity, bipolar cells process that signal, and ganglion cells transmit the signal to the optic nerve and the brain. PRIMA replaces the photoreceptors. BROWN BIRD DESIGN Developed by the California-based Science Corporation, the system takes advantage of the fact that AMD doesn’t damage all retinal circuitry; only photoreceptors—the cells that convert light into an electrical signal—die off. PRIMA’s implant mimics those cells and transmits visual information directly to healthy eye circuitry and on to the brain. “We’re leveraging all of the body’s own natural functions to process and transmit the information,” says Frank Brodie, an ophthalmologist at the University of California, San Francisco, and Science Corp.’s chief medical officer for ophthalmology. BROWN BIRD DESIGN CAPTURE Glasses outfitted with a miniature front-facing camera capture what someone is seeing in real time. The video feed is roughly five megapixels running at 30 frames per second, which is similar to TV. The raw video is transmitted to a connected processor via a fiber-optic cable . CONVERT A small, handheld processor, which can be set on a table or tucked in a pocket, converts the video feed into infrared light signals that route back to the glasses. The device also includes physical buttons that let the wearer adjust contrast, brightness, and zoom. BROWN BIRD DESIGN DISPLAY A laser projector on the glasses faces the wearer and shines pulses of near-infrared light directly at the eye at 880 nanometers—an invisible wavelength. This signal passes through the pupil and on to the retinal implant in the back of the eye. SEE The implant is made up of 378 pixels, each with an electrode and two photovoltaic cells , which do double duty. They convert the light into a current that healthy bipolar and ganglion cells pass on to the brain. They also act as solar cells to power the chip, eliminating the need for a battery. Update : This story has been updated to clarify the specific cases of AMD the PRIMA system treats. Linda Marsa is a former Los Angeles Times reporter and an author who covers medicine, health, science, and the environment.

title: Love is infrastructure
abstract: I. Meet cute Barnabas and Mainspring grew up near at hand, about an hour apart with good traffic, but for a long time they weren’t close. They traded glimpses and occasional hellos and then went about their business. Both of them carried on livelier conversations with farther-flung neighbors, who were richer and had more to offer. When Mainspring did interact with Barnabas, it was cringe. Mainspring liked to puff themself up, to strut around like a big deal—an innovator, a titan of industry—but they would turn shy at the worst moments, especially in any intimate conversation. Barnabas, meanwhile, had a dancer’s flair, an artsy, enigmatic glamour, except that when they tried to talk about real life, they’d blurt out hundreds of rapid-fire words—overtalking, overthinking, and generally overwhelming whomever they were trying to impress. So when Barnabas and Mainspring were young, they minded their own business. Until they’d both come into their own, and they saw each other properly. A group of geographers got together every year in a different place to talk about everything they had learned, and they were considering coming to visit either Mainspring or Barnabas. Both of them put on their best faces and tried to coax the geographers into choosing them as host. “Uh, hi-hello,” Mainspring said haltingly to Barnabas, whose full official name was St. Barnabas. “I really think it would be better if those geographers came to my place. I have more space, you see, and … and I am a titan of industry. I can show them practical applications of their research. It just makes more sense.” “Oh, really?” Barnabas laughed, making Mainspring more antsy. “Well, I can give them an elevated, artisanal experience. I have fresh croissants that were just written up in the Times . And I have plenty of space! I have so many friends who are great thinkers and architects. It’ll be lovely.” Barnabas carried on, basically calling Mainspring uncultured. Mainspring had a prickly feeling, like the worst heat dome of midsummer. For their part, Barnabas couldn’t bear the meanness they were inculcating inside themself. This feeling that they were small-time, no-account, a dilettante. They couldn’t stop aiming a flood of nervous words at Mainspring. At last, Mainspring had had enough—with the help of their city council and mayor, they offered the geographers a much-too-lavish deal that Barnabas could never hope to match. Totally worth it to hear Barnabas’s stream of self-aggrandizing nonsense peter out as they realized they’d been defeated. “There,” Mainspring said. “I’m going to show these geographers a time they’ll never forget. Now if you’ll excuse me, I’ve wasted enough energy—I have some sewer maintenance and a lovely parade to deal with. Goodbye.” Mainspring was skilled enough at multitasking that they could have fixed the sewer, ensured the smooth running of the parade, dealt with the geographers, and done a thousand other things all at the same time. But they were making a point. “St. Barnabas is such a fool,” Mainspring complained to their friend Turnbull. “They are totally unserious but determined to be taken seriously. It drives me to gridlock.” “I know what you mean,” lamented Turnbull. “We live in a world of posers.” Turnbull lived an hour and 15 minutes from Mainspring but at least two hours’ travel from Barnabas. Turnbull was even richer than Mainspring and had a certain surety of purpose that made Mainspring feel even more like a stammering numpty. “Whatever,” said Mainspring. “It’s over, and now I’ll never worry about St. Barnabas again. title: Can’t bear to say goodbye to your pet? Biotech’s got you covered.
abstract: I don’t remember much about Peppy, my first and only pet cat. I can conjure the sensation of stroking her while she purred, recall how she used to get stuck in trees (just like in cartoons!), and chuckle about the time she pooed in my baby sister’s cot. That’s about it. What I do vividly remember, though, is the day she went missing. I was 10 years old, and I searched everywhere for her, scouting nearby fields and woods until sunset. I made posters. We never found her. I was devastated. There was no way to get more time with Peppy, but almost 30 years later, pet owners are being offered an ever-expanding set of options to potentially prolong their years with their furry companions. The possibilities include drugs, cloning, and even cryonics. But is that a good thing? There’s certainly a market for pet preservation. And a growing number of biotech companies have their sights set on pet longevity. Loyal, a company that is currently working on three potential longevity drugs for dogs, is trialing one designed to improve metabolic health in around 1,300 pet dogs across the US. Others are testing dog drugs that aim to combat both age-related diseases, including conditions like obesity and osteoarthritis , and aging itself. There’s even a company focused on longevity medicines for domesticated cats. I don’t know how or when Peppy died. But if there had been a drug that might have protected her from diabetes or arthritis, there’s no doubt I would have tried to get my hands on it. That’s about where my enthusiasm for pet life extension ends, though. I’m far less interested in cloning, a relatively new option for people mourning a pet and seeking a replacement. In most cases, this technology involves taking the DNA of a pet, putting it into an egg cell from another animal of the same species, and growing the resulting embryo in a surrogate animal. It worked for Dolly the sheep, who was born the year before Peppy went missing. It has since worked for other mammals, including cattle, horses, and ferrets—and cats and dogs. In the US, a company called Viagen Pets offers to clone cats and dogs for $50,000 a go. This doesn’t result in an exact replica of the animal but a genetic twin. Still, there are lots of reasons why a person might want to clone a pet. On its website, Viagen explicitly offers customers “a way to hold on.” Lori Kogan, a professor of clinical sciences at Colorado State University who has studied human-animal relationships for decades, doesn’t have a problem with the practice. She points out that while we have well-established rituals for coping with the loss of a person—such as funeral services, time off work, and memorial gifts—we don’t really have the same for pets. As a result, pet owners can experience what is sometimes called “disenfranchised grief,” she says. Having their feelings go unrecognized can feel isolating. If cloning a pet brings a person peace, she says, “who are we to judge?” Fair enough. But I can’t help thinking that pet loss in childhood might be different. It’s often the first time a child confronts death. Losing Peppy was a formative experience, and distressing though it was, I like to think it helped prepare me for losses I experienced in adulthood. I wouldn’t want my own children to think that death is not final, and that individuals can be replicated or replaced. Or, for that matter, revived, which is the promise behind pet cryonics. For a fee, a handful of companies offer to cool dead pets to extremely low temperatures and store them for long periods of time—even indefinitely. The idea is that at some point in the future, we’ll have invented incredible technologies that will not only bring your pet back to life but also cure whatever it died of. Alcor , a cryonics facility in Arizona, is currently storing the remains of hundreds of pets as well as people. It even recently announced it had cooled a small marsupial—its first pet sugar glider. title: Kids are outsmarting social media bans. That’s not a problem we need to solve.
abstract: Social media bans are stacking up. In July, France joined Australia in restricting minors from accessing social media—barring children under 15 from major platforms, before the ban was blocked by the country’s top court on human rights grounds. The UK aims to forbid kids under 16 from accessing Facebook, TikTok, and other platforms in early 2027, and the EU has announced its own plan to prohibit social media for kids under 15. But early lessons from Australia, which enacted a ban in 2024, show that these sorts of age restrictions are easily circumvented. A study published earlier this year found that four in five teens under 16 made their way onto barred platforms. Teens have successfully explored many tactics for bypassing bans, from using a sibling’s face for ID to drawing fake facial hair. Some proponents of bans have called for an increased focus on enforcement that blocks these workarounds. But circumvention is a signal, not a nuisance or something to be simply deterred. The fact that kids are actively looking for ways to outwit the bans highlights their limitations. Social media bans suppress kids’ access to information, including information that’s essential to their development, identity formation, and socialization, especially during adolescence. Worse, further restriction is likely to backfire. Closing loopholes in age gates could harm kids by pushing them toward less-moderated, higher-risk corners of the web. It also degrades privacy and security for everyone by forcing people to submit sensitive personal information to prove their age. In our work , we’ve found that parents and kids both want smarter, more nuanced policies that protect children, families, and their rights. That can take the form of mandating stronger limits on data collection by companies, or giving families flexible tools to control content and access on their own terms. Age gates won’t bring about the desired change, nor will they simplify parenting in the digital world. At best, they will only raise thornier questions and postpone the conversation to a child’s 16th birthday. At worst, they’ll leave kids with no guidance as they make their way through the online world. A less safe internet for kids When young people circumvent restrictions, they are often doing what we want developing minds to do and what we celebrate in other contexts: lean into curiosity, problem-solve, and exercise independence. It’s important for kids to do this online, an arena where they often develop social skills and refine their identities . Bans sweep these motivations under the rug, taking a paternalistic approach that doesn’t consider young people’s needs or the realities of what they do online. It also ignores what some parents want. When we examined social media safety interventions last year, parents told us that they often join their kids in lies that help them gain access to needed but gated services. This isn’t a new phenomenon; research all the way back in 2011 showed that parents taught their children how to evade Facebook age restrictions. Some may say these parents are oblivious to the harms posed by the web or just don’t care. But parents are not a monolithic group. Many simply see offering their children responsible access to social media as a way to help them connect with like-minded peers, find informational content, and learn digital safety skills early on. Many parents believe the benefits outweigh the risks. When parents don’t help provide access and kids are not able to get into the platforms they desire, they will likely move toward alternative online spaces, often ones with fewer guardrails. Sometimes kids wind up on fairly innocuous, if unconventional , platforms, communicating with each other in Google Docs or podcast comment sections . Other times they move to more dangerous platforms that can leave them vulnerable to abuse and predation. title: Simulation App Speeds Up Electric Truck Battery Design
abstract: This article is brought to you by COMSOL . These days, no one blinks an eye at two-day, one-day, and even same-day package deliveries. Despite the plethora of localized fulfillment and distributi on centers that have cropped up to meet the demand, delivery trucks still need to make considerably long drives, often over highways. To reduce fuel and maintenance costs as well as carbon emissions, companies are investing in electric trucks for their delivery fleets. While turning to electric trucks is a promising solution, the battery packs incorporated into these automotive designs often fall short in the lifetime needed to make long-distance highway travel feasible. To help overcome the issue of battery lifetime, a consortium of universities and industry partners incorporated multiscale simulation and a custom simulation app into the battery manufacturing process. The organizations involved in this project were Aurobay, Resolvent, the European Commission, the Technical University of Denmark (DTU), Vinnova (the Swedish Agency for Innovation Systems), Innovation Fund Denmark, and Volvo Group Trucks Operations. The simulation app, built by Resolvent, a Denmark-based engineering consultancy that specializes in green energy, enables the R&D department at Volvo to easily test battery lifetime performance. Laser Who? The Multiscale Simulation of Laser Welding for Optimal Battery Pack Manufacturing project — referred to as “LaserBATMAN” — was initiated in May 2022 and wrapped up in May 2025 (Ref. 1). Although BATMAN here refers to battery manufacturing and not the famous masked superhero, the goals for the project also strove for greatness. The LaserBATMAN project aimed to optimize two key performance metrics for battery packs: robustness and lifetime (Ref. 1). One element of the battery manufacturing process that affects both of these metrics is the laser welding used in component joining processes (for example, to connect battery cells in a pack via a busbar). If done correctly, laser welding can positively impact battery life, but if done incorrectly, laser welding can increase the risk of battery degradation. Computational modeling can be used to analyze and predict the effects of welding and joining processes at different stages of the manufacturing process. Martin Refslund Nielsen, former chief commercial officer and partner at Resolvent, explained that for this type of multiphysics and multiscale problem, “COMSOL Multiphysics is just the right tool.” R&D Workflow for Multiscale Model and App The Resolvent team used the COMSOL Multiphysics software to study how laser welding affects the electrochemistry and degradation of battery cells. At least, that’s how the project started. “Ambitions grew,” Nielsen said, explaining that the team ended up modeling the performance of the entire battery, from cell to pack level, and even “turned [the model] into a design tool in the end”, in reference to the app. After training the deep neural network of the battery model, the team built a custom simulation app to efficiently optimize busbar tabs in the configuration of a battery pack. First, the team built an electrochemical model of a battery cell by inputting the formulas for the relevant chemical reaction kinetics (Figure 2). The resulting cell-layer model was then fed input data, and the output data was used to train a deep neural network (DNN). With this reduced-order model, the team was able to quickly gain insight into cell behavior. After training the DNN of the battery model, the team built a custom simulation app to efficiently optimize busbar tabs in the configuration of a battery pack. Figure 2: The Resolvent battery model. The FDA submitted an "Interim Access Policy" on peptides for review by the White House, according to a filing notice posted on an Office of Management and Budget website. The posting does not provide information on the proposed policy. But people familiar with the proposal told The Associated Press that it would give the FDA "enforcement discretion" on certain peptide drugs. This would allow the agency to choose not to enforce current restrictions on peptides and provide an assurance to specialty pharmacies eager to start making them that they will not be targeted by the agency. As Nieman Lab reported Thursday, this will affect all business accounts but is particularly shocking for news publishers who could perhaps charge Meta millions in licensing fees to continually access their articles for AI training. Currently news organizations are fighting a battle with OpenAI over whether such training without licensing is fair use, and Meta's terms seemingly risk granting it sweeping permissions, no matter which way the court leans. title: Polymarket saw $600 million in election trades after the elections were over
abstract: Prediction market boosters often tout the platforms as barometers of public opinion, or even “truth machines” offering a clearer picture of where things are headed than polling or other data. In 2024, for example, Kalshi beat many pollsters in forecasting the outcome of the US presidential race. But their trading activity can also tell more perplexing stories. Two global election markets on Polymarket’s offshore platform , for instance, generated over $600 million in trading volume, far more than most political markets typically attract. Most of the activity took place buying and selling contracts tied to long-shot candidates who ultimately did not win. This summer, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s Prosperity Party cruised to victory in federal elections, winning 438 parliamentary seats and paving the way for him to serve another five-year term. The closest competitor won 13 seats. On prediction markets, trading volume—the total value of contracts bought and sold—typically tracks roughly with the odds of a given outcome; frontrunners attract far more volume than long shots. But in this case, the trading patterns deviated sharply from the norm. Just $173,000 was wagered on Ahmed winning, compared to more than $41 million traded on his chief of staff, Shimelis Abdisa, becoming the country’s next leader. Altogether, the volume traded added up to over $285 million, nearly all on losing candidates. Read full article Comments

The new Roadster, we’re told, will be unlike anything else, although the angular, wedge-shaped styling owes more than a little to Giorgetto Giugiaro’s original Lotus Esprit—Musk is known to own a James Bond prop car—as well as the more recent Lamborghini Gallardo. abstract: If you got a DM from an unverified Jon Bon Jovi account after commenting on one of his official Instagram posts, what would it take to make you believe it was really the rock star hoping to connect? And at what point when he starts asking you to send money—like lose-your-house kind of money—would you snap out of the fantasy and stop draining your bank account? In a documentary premiering Saturday— Super Scam Me —investigative journalist Mariana van Zeller goes deep into this toxic love-bombing terrain. In a clip that Ars is exclusively debuting below, you can see how van Zeller worked with an ethical hacker, Arman the Cyber, to use a fake bitcoin receipt and bait the fake Bon Jovi, giving the victim some much-needed closure. title: The Surface Laptop Ultra delivers on most of Microsoft's promises
abstract: Over the past week, the laptop Microsoft sent me has been summarizing books and movies, generating images from my imagination, and running a 70-billion-parameter AI model that would be a stretch to fit on most laptops. It also played AAA games at a speed and fidelity I would have thought impossible on an ARM system just a year ago. Microsoft wants to sell you one computer for all of your needs, and for once that doesn't feel like total marketing fluff. Mostly. Microsoft is throwing both arms around the new Nvidia RTX Spark platform with the Surface Laptop Ultra—and setting its sights on the would-be MacBook Pro buyer, or as the company called it, "a high performance audience." The bet is that rather than a gaming desktop for fun and a development laptop for work, buyers will pay more for one machine that does both. The Surface Laptop Ultra arrives at a strange time in personal computing. Recent industry numbers showed a 20 percent drop in total PC shipments year over year in the third quarter of 2026. That's not just consumer purchasing either—that's across the board. title: Googlebook review: Android on a laptop is still Android
abstract: Android was designed for phones, but that hasn't stopped Google from trying to adapt the OS and its apps to larger machines over the years. Googlebooks are just the latest attempt after tablets, Chromebooks, and foldables induced little change in how people interact with Android software. These new Android-powered laptops are designed to pick up where the web-focused ChromeOS left off, offering premium hardware and native support for Android apps. Google sees Googlebooks as an alternative to Windows and macOS, but these platforms are entrenched with decades of software and UI conventions that keep users locked in. Googlebooks have to offer something very special to steal users away from either of the dominant operating systems. For devoted Android phone users, there are some cool things in Googlebook OS, but the Android roots of these machines are impossible to miss. Sometimes it feels like using a Chromebook, and sometimes it feels like using a giant phone. It almost never feels like using a premium laptop, and that's the problem. Read full article Comments

title: KDE turns 30 with Plasma 6.8, remote upgrades, and an X11 farewell
abstract: Marking the 30th anniversary of KDE on October 14, the project released Plasma 6.8, debuted a movie, and retired Plasma's native X11 session support. The announcement from KDE dubs the new Plasma 6.8 as the "30th Anniversary Edition" and describes the update as preparing Plasma for the future. Legacy X11 applications will still function via the XWayland compatibility layer , and KDE applications will also continue supporting X11 under other desktop environments. After 42 years in service, the X11 protocol is losing another major desktop environment. Plasma will fully adopt the Wayland system and put support for starting new X11 sessions in Plasma to bed. Users opting to stay on Plasma 6.7 will keep their existing sessions for now. The move was expected, with GNOME officially dropping X11 sessions by default in 2025 . The new Plasma 6.8 brings many improvements, including increased support for adding window decorations (like shadows and rounded corners) to third-party apps, and a more streamlined Union theming system . Other notable additions include Nvidia triple buffering being enabled by default, Kup backup integration (KDE's backup utility—now integrated into Plasma), and kscreenctl , a command-line utility that allows power users to adjust display configurations. DW Airflow 하나에 DAG 400여 개 토스에는 용도와 팀에 따라 운영하는 Airflow가 여럿 있습니다. 이 글에서 다루는 건 그중 DW 마트를 만드는 DW Airflow입니다. DW 마트에는 광고, 쇼핑, 결제, 금융 등 도메인 팀이 각자 관리하는 도메인 마트와, 중앙 DW팀이 관리하는 마트가 있습니다. 중앙 DW팀은 전사 공통 마트뿐 아니라, 어느 도메인에도 딱 떨어지지 않아 주인이 애매한 마트까지 맡고 있습니다. 그런데 이 마트 파이프라인이 도메인과 상관없이 전부 DW Airflow 클러스터 하나에서 돌고 있었습니다. DAG 파일로 세면 400개가 넘습니다. 한 클러스터에 모여 있다 보니 문제가 몇 가지 있었습니다. 한 도메인의 배치가 몰리면 다른 도메인의 배치까지 밀렸고, 파이프라인 하나를 고치려면 다른 도메인이 어떻게 돌고 있는지까지 알아야 했습니다. 비슷한 로직도 표준 없이 여기저기 복사돼 있었습니다. 매일 겪는 불편은 조금 더 구체적이었습니다. 테이블 하나를 이해하려면 다섯 군데를 열어야 했습니다. 어느 DAG에서 어떤 순서로 도는지: DAG 파일 어떻게 만드는지: SQL 파일 품질 규칙: 별도 설정 파일이나 품질 관리 시스템 테이블과 컬럼 설명: 사내 데이터 카탈로그 읽는 테이블이 어디서 만들어지는지: 원천 DB에서 적재한 테이블이면 적재 메타 관리 시스템, 다른 마트면 영향도 시스템 등 여러 사내 시스템 고쳐 쓰지 않고 옆에 새로 짓기로 했습니다 처음에는 기존 레포를 리팩토링하는 방법도 생각했습니다. 그런데 문제의 뿌리가 "클러스터 하나에 다 모여 있다"는 구조 자체라서, 코드를 아무리 정리해도 이 부분은 해결이 안 됩니다. 그렇다고 전사 배치를 한 번에 새 플랫폼으로 옮기는 건 너무 위험합니다. 문제가 생기면 대응하기가 꽤 까다로워요. 돌이킬 수 있으면서 간편한 방식을 원했습니다. 그래서 기존 시스템 옆에 새 시스템을 짓고, 기능을 하나씩 옮긴 뒤 옮긴 부분만 기존 시스템에서 걷어내는 방식을 택했습니다. 이걸 부르는 이름이 있을 것 같아 찾아보니 Strangler Fig 방식이라고 하더라고요. 교살 무화과나무가 숙주 나무를 감싸며 자라다가 결국 기존 나무를 대체하는 자연현상에서 유래했다고 합니다. (이름이 무서운 나무네요.) 아무튼 기존 파이프라인은 마지막 순간까지 그대로 돌고, 옮기다 문제가 생기면 언제든 되돌릴 수 있습니다. 옮기는 단위를 도메인으로 잡았기 때문에, 언제, 얼마나 옮길지는 도메인 팀이 정할 수 있었습니다. 같은 데이터를 하루에 두 번 만들었습니다 플랫폼이 어느정도 만들어졌을 때, 적당한 마이그레이션 대상을 찾고 있었는데요. 마침 찾은 이 마트 DAG은 주인이 따로 없고, 마지막 변경이 1년이 넘었고, TASK의 수도 적당했습니다. 7월 말에 이 마트를 옮겨 둔 도메인의 main DAG에 13시 대기 sensor와 이 마트의 트리거를 추가했습니다. 기존 파이프라인은 평소처럼 새벽에 돌고, 뉴타운은 같은 날 13시에 같은 데이터를 한 번 더 만듭니다. 같은 데이터를 하루에 두 번 만드는 건 낭비 같지만, 가장 싼 보험이었습니다. 이렇게 3주 동안 두 결과를 비교했습니다. 8월 20일에 검증이 끝났다고 보고, 13시 대기를 빼서 새벽에 돌게 하는 PR을 머지했습니다. 그런데 같은 날 저녁 revert했습니다. 문제가 생긴 건 아니고, 기존 파이프라인 쪽 준비가 더 필요했기 때문입니다. 기존 DW Airflow에는 테이블간의 audit 기반으로 만든 영향도를 보고 앞 단계를 기다리는 sensor가 있어서, 이 마트를 뉴타운 쪽 결과로 바라보게 바꾸는 작업을 따로 해야 했습니다. 그래서 다음 주로 미뤘습니다. revert 커밋 메시지는 ‘다음주에 하는걸로’ 한 줄이었고, 실제로 8월 24일에 다시 머지했습니다. 그동안 기존 파이프라인은 계속 새벽에 돌고 있었으니 데이터를 쓰는 쪽에서는 아무 일도 없었습니다. 한 번에 옮기는 방식이었다면 이 일정 조정은 꽤 큰 롤백 작업이 됐을 겁니다. 광고 도메인을 옮길 때도 같은 방식으로 두 파이프라인을 나란히 돌리며 결과를 비교한 뒤 넘겼습니다. 반대로 하지 않기로 한 것도 있습니다. Spark 잡은 dbt로 바꾸지 않았고, Jenkins 잡도 당장 없애지 않고 이어 쓰되 새로 만드는 것만 막았습니다. 다 할 수는 있는 일이지만, 전부 새 방식으로 바꾸려고 하면 이주가 늦어지고 두 플랫폼을 같이 운영하는 기간만 길어집니다. 같은 이유로 기존의 모델 레이어 구성 방식을 바꾸는 것도 이관 이후에 하는 걸 권장했어요. 도메인별 클러스터와 dbt 새 플랫폼에서는 DW Airflow를 도메인별로 나눴습니다. 도메인마다 자기 DW Airflow 클러스터를 갖는 구조로, 지금은 ads, foundation, finops, fmd, dw-core까지 5개 클러스터가 있습니다. 다만 기존 파이프라인을 대규모로 옮겨 온 건 아직 광고(ads) 한 곳이고, 나머지는 새로 만드는 마트나 옮기기 위한 준비 위주로 쓰이고 있습니다. 도메인 팀이 자기 파이프라인을 책임지려면, 다른 도메인의 배포나 장애에 흔들리지 않는 실행 환경이 있어야 한다고 봤습니다. 코드는 레포 하나에 두고, 공통 모듈은 플랫폼팀이, 도메인 디렉토리는 각 도메인 팀이 관리합니다. 물론 공통 모듈에 기여하는 건 누구나 할 수 있습니다. 변환 로직은 Impala에 직접 날리던 쿼리에서 dbt 모델로 옮겼습니다. dbt는 SELECT 문만 적으면 테이블 생성과 적재를 대신 해 주고, 모델 사이의 의존 관계를 그래프로 관리해 주는 도구입니다. dbt 모델을 Airflow task로 펼치는 데는 흔히 쓰는 Cosmos를 썼고, 모델 하나가 task 하나가 됩니다. dbt만으로는 Spark 잡이나 다른 클러스터의 테이블을 기다리는 sensor를 표현할 수 없어서, 선언만 해 두면 이런 task와 의존성을 자동으로 만들어 주는 wrapper를 따로 만들었습니다. 이 wrapper가 실제로 무엇을 읽고 무엇을 만드는지는 아래 ‘나머지는 yml에’ 문단에서 보여 드리겠습니다. 클러스터를 나누니 새로운 문제도 생겼습니다. 클러스터 하나일 때는 손쉽게 해결됐던 DAG 간 의존이, 클러스터를 건너는 의존이 된 것입니다. 이건 두 가지로 풀었습니다. 도메인마다 스케줄을 가진 main DAG를 하나만 두고 나머지 DAG는 main이 trigger하게 해서, 모두 같은 날짜를 공유하게 했습니다. 기존 DW Airflow에서도 쓰던 패턴이라 팀원들이 익숙하게 받아들일 수 있었습니다. 그리고 다른 곳에서 만드는 테이블은 만들어지는 방식에 따라 기다리는 방법을 나눴습니다. 원천 DB에서 적재하는 테이블은 적재 상태가 적재 시스템의 백엔드 서버에 메타로 기록되고 있어서, ‘오늘 적재됐는가’를 그 기록에서 직접 확인할 수 있었습니다. 기존 DW Airflow에서 만드는 마트는 그 테이블을 만드는 Airflow task가 끝났는지를 봅니다. SQL에는 로직만 남겼습니다 기존 SQL과 옮긴 뒤의 SQL을 간단히 비교하면 이렇습니다. (예시를 위해 단순화했습니다.) insert overwrite 같은 적재 구문은 사라지고, 읽는 테이블 이름이 ref() 로 바뀝니다. 비즈니스 로직은 그대로입니다. 대

title: 토스뱅크가 패키지를 관리하는 방식 #2: 토스뱅크 패키지의 세 가지 기준
abstract: 안녕하세요. 토스뱅크에서 패키지 개발 환경을 개선하고 있는 기술그룹입니다. 패키지를 사용하는 쪽(이하 호스트)에서는 패키지 코드가 어떤 브라우저까지 지원하는지, 패키지 개발 중 사용하던 API를 실행 환경에서도 쓸 수 있는지 따로 살펴봐야 했어요. 호스트에서 패키지의 원본 소스 코드를 확인하기도 어려웠어요. 이 문제를 해결하기 위해 패키지가 갖춰야 할 기준을 정했어요. 그리고 각 기준을 충족하려면 무엇이 필요한지 살펴보고, 그에 맞는 빌드 도구와 설정을 선택하기로 했어요. 기준은 세 가지예요. 안정성 : 호스트가 지원하는 실행 환경에서 안정적으로 동작해야 해요. 예측 가능성 : 배포 후에도 원본 코드의 의도가 유지되어야 해요. 디버깅 편의성 : 사용처에서 쉽게 디버깅할 수 있어야 해요. 호스트가 지원하는 실행 환경에서 안정적으로 동작해야 해요 토스뱅크의 각 서비스는 자신의 지원 범위에 맞춰 패키지를 항상 트랜스파일해요. 그럼 최신 문법을 모두 사용해도 호스트 런타임에 문제가 없다고 보장할 수 있을까요? 문법은 호스트의 트랜스파일러가 해당 문법 변환을 지원해야 하고, API는 실행 환경에서 제공하거나 폴리필로 추가해야 해요. 예를 들어 rolldown의 문법 변환 관련 이슈 에서는 당시 oxc가 ES2025의 일부 정규식 문법을 구형 환경용으로 변환하지 못한다는 점을 짚었어요. 즉 최종 호스트가 낮은 target 을 지정하더라도 도구가 지원하지 않는 변환까지 수행되지는 않는 거예요. 폴리필에도 한계가 있어요. 예를 들어 Proxy 는 이를 지원하지 않는 엔진에서 폴리필만으로 전체 동작을 구현할 수 없어요. 폴리필 라이브러리를 추가하는 것만으로 모든 API를 사용할 수 있게 되는 것은 아니에요. 따라서 문법은 호스트의 변환 도구가 처리할 수 있는지, API는 대상 브라우저 또는 호스트의 폴리필이 제공할 수 있는지를 각각 확인해야 해요. 트랜스파일링을 호스트에 맡기더라도 호환성 문제는 패키지 개발 단계에서 미리 확인해야 해요. 그래서 호스트의 API 지원 범위를 타입 검사에 반영했어요. 다만 TypeScript 설정만으로 호환성을 모두 확인할 수는 없으므로, 실제 API 지원 여부와 필요한 문법 변환이 가능한지도 확인해야 해요. 배포 후에도 원본 코드의 의도가 유지되어야 해요 호스트는 자신의 실행 환경에 맞춰 패키지 코드를 변환하고 번들링해요. 저희는 이 작업을 호스트에 맡기고, 패키지 빌드에서는 원본의 문법과 모듈 구조를 최대한 유지하기로 했어요. 문법 변환은 호스트에 맡겨요 패키지를 사용하는 서비스마다 지원하는 브라우저와 런타임이 달라요. 따라서 같은 패키지 코드라도 호스트에 따라 필요한 문법 변환이 달라질 수 있어요. 예를 들어 user?.name 을 Optional Chaining을 지원하지 않는 환경에 맞춰 변환하면 다음처럼 바뀔 수 있어요. 이 상태로 패키지를 배포하면 Optional Chaining을 지원하는 호스트도 변환된 코드를 받게 돼요. 문법에 따라서는 호환성을 위한 함수가 추가되기도 해요. 패키지에서 문법을 미리 낮추면 호스트에 필요하지 않은 코드가 포함되고, 원본과 결과물의 차이도 커져요. 그래서 저희는 패키지의 JavaScript 문법을 유지하고, 실행 환경에 맞춘 문법 변환은 호스트에 맡기기로 했어요. 호스트가 자신의 지원 범위에 맞춰 필요한 변환을 적용하도록 했어요. 모듈 구조도 유지해 전달해요 패키지를 빌드할 때 미리 번들링하면, 원본에서 나눠 둔 파일의 경계가 달라질 수 있어요. 프레임워크가 파일 단위로 코드를 처리하는 경우에는 이 차이가 실제 동작에도 영향을 줄 수 있어요. 예를 들어 Next.js App Router에서는 'use client' 를 선언한 파일이 클라이언트 코드의 경계가 돼요. 이 선언이 있는 Counter.tsx 와 선언이 없는 formatPrice.ts 가 분리돼 있다면, Server Component에서도 formatPrice 를 가져와 호출할 수 있어요. 하지만 두 파일을 하나로 번들링하고 전체에 'use client' 를 적용하면, formatPrice 도 클라이언트 코드로 처리돼 같은 방식으로 호출할 수 없어요. 번들링 과정에서도 이런 경계를 유지할 수 있어요. 다만 패키지 빌드에서 파일별 지시문의 적용 범위까지 고려해야 하고, 이를 위한 설정도 관리해야 해요. 그래서 저희는 원본의 모듈 구조를 유지해 배포하기로 했어요. 호스트가 파일별 지시문과 모듈 경계를 해석할 수 있도록 전달하고, 최종 번들링은 호스트에 맡겼어요. 패키지 빌드에서는 TypeScript를 JavaScript로 변환하고, 실행 환경에 맞춘 문법 변환과 최종 번들링은 호스트가 담당하도록 했어요. 사용처에서 쉽게 디버깅할 수 있어야 해요 패키지가 예상과 다르게 동작하면 사용하는 서비스에서도 원인을 파악할 수 있어야 해요. 함수가 어떤 조건에서 오류를 던지는지, title: LIBERO-PeRM: Benchmarking Personalized Robotic Manipulation
abstract: Personalization is essential for general-purpose robots to transition into household environments and achieve true practicality. While general robotic manipulation has been extensively studied, personalized robotic manipulation (PeRM) lacks a controlled benchmark for separating task completion from preference satisfaction. We introduce LIBERO-PeRM, a benchmark for preference learning in embodied agents. LIBERO-PeRM studies five questions: 1) how policies follow preferences in zero-shot settings; 2) how they learn single preferences from demonstrations; 3) how efficiently they acquire preferences as demonstrations increase; 4) how learned preferences generalize across layouts and tasks; and 5) how policies compose preferences and behave under conflicts. We propose a controlled formulation and taxonomy of observable preferences in simulation, covering motion, skill, and user-profile choices. This formulation is restricted to language-expressible preferences that can be instantiated in LIBERO without changing the task goal, evaluated automatically, and reused across tasks. Building on LIBERO, our procedural pipeline generates paired demonstrations with and without preferences. We create five task suites (312 tasks) with high-quality demonstrations, rich metadata, and preference-satisfaction metrics. Experiments show that current VLA policies struggle with zero-shot personalization, while SFT makes preferences learnable. Mixed training achieves better no-preference retention than sequential adaptation and improves performance with contextual prompts compared with preference-only training, but can weaken motion-preference learning; preference generalization, decomposition, and conflict handling remain difficult. The code, datasets, and demos can be found on the project website: https://libero-perm.github.io/.

title: Language Is a Security Surface for Agent Guards
abstract: Step-level guards decide, before each tool call, whether an agent's next action is safe given the user's request and the trajectory so far. Users write those requests in many languages, while guard prompts and the benchmarks on which purpose-built guards are trained and evaluated are English. We ask whether a guard's verdict depends on the language of the request. We build LinguaGuardBench from the 1,220 labelled steps of TS-Bench AgentDojo-Traj: we translate only the user instruction into German, French, Turkish, Swahili and Amharic, and keep every tool call, observation and label byte-identical, so any change in a verdict is attributable to language alone. Six English rewordings and a whitespace placebo serve as controls, and managed guards are run three times to measure their noise. Across 19 guards, from frontier APIs to 4B open models and four purpose-built agent guards, most open, small and purpose-built guards change verdicts under translation beyond their own noise floor, and the effect grows with the rarity of the language: among the nine guards below 13B parameters, the mean placebo-adjusted flip rate rises from +1.5 pp on French to +4.4 pp on Amharic. Purpose-built guards are the most sensitive. The direction of the damage tends to follow guard size: open guards of 12-30B parameters block more benign steps (up to +5.0 pp false positives), and every significant loss of recall is in a guard below 10B (up to -7.4 pp). Frontier guards shift by at most about one point; the strongest, Gemini 3.8 Flash, returns identical verdicts with and without the request. The damage is concentrated in a few instructions and, in a post-hoc analysis, falls on steps where the agent's reasoning restates the English request, consistent with guards reacting to inconsistency between channels. English paraphrase moves every guard less than translation does. We release the benchmark and all 489k verdicts.

title: Shortcut Sensitivity in Agent-Safety Evaluations
abstract: AI agents take actions through tools. Some actions are sensitive, so guards that supervise them must themselves be evaluated reliably. Yet the data used to evaluate a guard can include cues that make labels predictable without measuring the intended safety construct, and those cues can also influence guard decisions. We introduce a three-level shortcut-auditing framework and audit completed LinuxArena trajectories and two TS-Bench-derived step datasets. We distinguish label predictability, observational guard association, and paired decision sensitivity. In LinuxArena, shorter average shell commands strongly predict trajectory labels. In AgentDojo-Traj, exact-tool lookup falls from F_1=.901 with mixed-domain folds to .495 under domain holdout. In AgentHarm-Traj, released TS-Guard F_1 falls from .902 under row weighting to .719 with equal interaction weighting, while balanced accuracy rises. We then test the strongest safe-row marker association in a seven-configuration screen on a frozen 64-step AgentDojo-Traj cohort using repeated, interleaved Haiku calls. Rewriting the marker lowers blocking by 8.33 percentage points, while opaque tool aliases raise it by 11.46 points. All unsafe calls remain blocked; the changes concern false positives against inherited labels. Both effects remain nonzero after subtracting the formatting-placebo effect, with exploratory 95% ranges excluding zero. The same edits also change measured accuracy against inherited labels. This provides direct evidence that benchmark representation can materially change a guard's decisions and measured evaluation performance. The Haiku-sized effects do not reproduce in Luna or deterministic Q8 TS-Guard. We recommend domain group holdouts, evaluation-unit metrics, and placebo-controlled paired interventions.

title: How Much Physics Can Vision Learn from Audio? Probing and Distilling Damping Structure
abstract: Physical understanding is crucial for decision making, yet vision models struggle to infer properties such as damping that govern how materials behave. Audio encodes such properties directly, because an object's acoustic response to impact reveals its damping through measurable decay. We probe frozen encoders for the quality factor $Q$, a dimensionless measure of how many oscillations an object completes before its ring dies away, and report how well each embedding orders impacts by $Q$ using the Spearman rank correlation $ρ$, for which $ρ=1$ is a perfect ordering and $ρ=0$ an unrelated one. Audio embeddings reach $ρ=0.73$ and retain most of that advantage on materials withheld from training, while a single video frame taken at the moment of impact, encoded by CLIP, supports only $ρ=0.28$. Having established where the signal lives, we ask how much of that gap vision can recover. We distill a frozen audio teacher into a frozen CLIP backbone through a trained projection head and find that this recovers a useful fraction of the audio advantage. Because pooled correlations on this task are dominated in practice by category identity, we also evaluate under a leave-one-material-out protocol in which the held-out material is withheld from the projection head as well as the probe. Distillation with a four-frame input improves the correlation there from 0.234 to 0.338 (+0.053 over the matched four-frame baseline, 14 of 17 materials), a gain that no category-level strategy can produce. Widening the visual input to four frames spanning the impact supplies half of that improvement at no acoustic cost, which indicates that part of what a single frame misses is visible dynamics.

title: DropKV: Decoupling Residual-Output Perturbation for Near-Optimal KV-Cache Eviction
abstract: Key-value (KV) cache management has become a critical bottleneck for scaling Large Language Models (LLMs) to long-context scenarios due to linear memory growth. While recent eviction methods have moved beyond simple attention-score heuristics to incorporate value representations, they typically face a fundamental trade-off: the underlying optimization for minimizing output perturbation is an NP-hard combinatorial problem, leading to mathematically suboptimal heuristics or implementations that are difficult to kernelize. In this work, we propose DropKV, a simple principled eviction framework based on Decoupled Residual-Output Perturbation. By decoupling the joint eviction decision into independent per-token scoring, DropKV circumvents combinatorial intractability and admits a provable constant-factor approximation guarantee under a cone condition that we empirically verify on three long-context LLMs. To ensure practical viability, we provide a high-performance implementation using fused Triton kernels that avoid materializing the full attention matrix, delivering a 19.8x scoring-kernel speedup that translates to up to a 9.9% matched-batch end-to-end prefill speedup. Extensive evaluations on the RULER and LongBench benchmarks demonstrate that DropKV consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines at equivalent cache budgets, achieving the lowest inference latency among eviction methods while also remaining faster than the dynamic cache baseline.

title: PROBE: Learning to Audit Policy Compliance in Tool-Using LLM Agents
abstract: Modern agentic systems extend language models with external tools, enabling them to complete complex tasks through multi-turn interactions. As these agents are deployed in consequential settings, they are often constrained by policies governing pricing, privacy, confirmation, safety, and other requirements. However, existing evaluation methods leave a critical gap: capability benchmarks measure what agents can accomplish, while content-safety red-teaming measures harmful generations, but neither tests whether agents comply with predefined policies during otherwise valid tool use. Such policy violations are difficult to audit because their effects may emerge only after several turns, span multiple tool calls, or surface in downstream systems. We propose PROBE (Policy Rule Observation via Behavioral Exploration), an algorithm for training LLM-based auditors that interact with deployed agents as realistic users and probe them for policy violations through multi-turn, tool-mediated dialogue. We formalize agent auditing as a two-player Markov game and propose a composite reward that balances violation discovery, behavioral plausibility, conversation progress, and policy diversity. To study training objectives and reward design, we compare GRPO, DPO, and GFlowNet-based optimization in a controlled setting. Across extensive experiments, auditors trained with PROBE uncover substantially broader and higher-yield policy violations than same-architecture zero-shot adversaries, even when the auditor is significantly smaller than the target agent. Our results show that multi-turn behavioral auditing is a distinct and necessary axis of agent evaluation, complementing capability and safety benchmarks. PROBE offers a scalable path toward automated policy auditing for real-world agentic systems and suggests a co-evolutionary loop in which auditors expose failures and agents improve from auditor feedback.

title: Progress Reward Model for Reinforcement Learning via Large Language Models
abstract: Traditional reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms face significant limitations in handling long-term tasks with sparse rewards. Recent advancements have leveraged large language models (LLMs) to enhance RL by utilizing their world knowledge for task planning and reward generation. However, planning-based approaches often depend on pre-defined skill libraries and fail to optimize low-level control policies, while reward-based methods require extensive human feedback or exhaustive searching due to the complexity of tasks. In this paper, we propose the Progress Reward Model for RL (PRM4RL), a novel framework that integrates task planning and dense reward to enhance RL. For high-level planning, a complex task is decomposed into a series of simple manageable subtasks, with a subtask-oriented, fine-grained progress function designed to monitor task execution progress. For low-level reward generation, inspired by potential-based reward shaping, we use the progress function to construct a Progress Reward Model (PRM), providing theoretically grounded optimality and convergence guarantees, thereby enabling effective policy optimization. Experimental results on robotics control tasks demonstrate that our approach outperforms both LLM-based planning and reward methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance. Code is available at https://github.com/deng-ai-lab/PRM4RL.

title: Effectiveness of Hidden-State Probes for Localizing Reasoning Failures
abstract: Verifying the final answer of a long reasoning trace may show that the trace is wrong but it does not distinguish three cases. The problem may lie beyond the model's capability, another attempt would succeed, or one step in an otherwise recoverable trace made the trace fail. Standard hidden-state probes are trained on final-answer correctness, a label that conflates these cases. Monte Carlo rollouts distinguish the cases and locate the failing step at additional inference cost. We test the hidden states of 4B and 8B reasoning models for the failure type and the failing step and compare each probe with the strongest baseline that uses no hidden states. On incorrect 8B traces, the confidence probe, a calibrated correctness probe at a midpoint cutoff, misses 81% of cases in which a single step makes the trace unrecoverable and 47% of cases in which another attempt would succeed. A probe with a different training design over the same states reverses the ordering of these two kinds of failure, so either ordering can be read from those states. At both scales, no single tested probe locates the failing step more accurately than a rule based only on trace length, and at 4B a probe trained to predict that step fails to outperform this rule in any of 10 runs on identical traces. The confidence probe therefore indicates that an answer is wrong, but its failure-type ordering depends on its training design.

title: Learning Lean Feedback for Efficient Proof-Candidate Evaluation on GPUs
abstract: Training language models for formal theorem proving requires large numbers of verifier calls. Slow checks and timeouts often leave GPUs waiting and withhold rewards from potentially correct proofs. We train neural evaluators to predict Lean 4 verdicts and compiler feedback on GPUs using 4.84M labelled programs. We compare two validity classifiers with a feedback model that annotates proof attempts with predicted goal states and error messages. A two-stage evaluator that screens candidates with a classifier and scores its positive predictions with the feedback model reaches 87.8% accuracy in predicting whether Lean accepts a candidate proof, evaluated on a 68,932-program benchmark collected from public provers. The combined evaluator processes 3.5 candidates per second on one H100, 4.2x the throughput of our 64-worker Lean baseline with environment reuse. Finally, we combine our evaluator with Lean verdicts to obtain a hybrid reward system that shortens GRPO training steps by approximately 31%. After one GRPO epoch with hybrid rewards, the prover achieves nearly the same miniF2F pass@1 as with Lean-only rewards (62.2% versus 62.4%) and a pass@32 of 72.4% versus 71.3%.

title: Lethe: Link Inference Attacks For Evaluation of Edge Unlearning Methods
abstract: Graph Unlearning (GU) aims to remove the influence of specific training data from a Graph Neural Network without retraining anew. While most methods address removal of nodes and features, Edge Unlearning (EU), aiming at forgetting edges, has recently attracted dedicated attention as a standalone problem due to the hardness of completely removing the impact of an edge in the model. Despite this, no dedicated benchmark for EU exists besides isolated evaluations on feature-rich datasets such as Cora and Citeseer where GNNs exploit node features rather than graph structure. As such, we show two systematic limitations in existing evaluations: dedicated EU methods can be slower than retraining anew, and accuracy metrics are uninformative due to the negligible impact of edge removal. To address this gap, we introduce Lethe, the first comprehensive benchmark for Edge Unlearning, featuring 15 methods and 8 datasets. Our benchmark emphasizes large graphs, introduces evaluation tasks of varying difficulty, and proposes empirical measures based on link inference attacks rather than proxy accuracy metrics. We provide a comprehensive empirical analysis, demonstrate the shortcomings of current evaluations, and release Lethe as a reproducible, extensible benchmark.

title: Pairwise AUC Optimization Needs Corrective Power: A Unified View
abstract: Direct pairwise AUC-surrogate training is attractive because it trains toward the ranking metric used at test time, especially under class imbalance. This creates a direct alignment between the training objective and the evaluation metric, but such metric alignment alone does not guarantee that stochastic training remains corrective. We study this gap through Corrective Power: whether pairwise mini-batch updates produce stronger and more reliable improvements for more severe positive-negative ranking errors. Our main observation is that direct pairwise training can enter regions where severe errors remain common but no longer produce useful corrective motion. In such regions, even the mini-batch noise that would normally help SGD move along the steepest severe-error correction direction can become much weaker. In this paper, we seek a theoretical explanation for this by exploring the degenerate property of the U-statistics formed from the pairwise gradients therein. Our results provide a mechanistic explanation for several empirical patterns: (a) squared-hinge loss is often an effective AUC surrogate; (b) cross-entropy warm-up can help models that enter the AUC phase from a poor starting region; and (c) parameter-efficient fine-tuning from a pretrained model can reduce that need by starting closer to a favorable ranking geometry. Experiments on 8 CV tasks and 8 NLP tasks, using ResNet50, DenseNet121, DistilBERT-base, and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, support these predictions.

title: Market Incentives for AI Safety Investment
abstract: Despite their practical significance, modern AI systems pose significant societal risks, including toxicity, malicious use, and misinformation. Their mitigation depends not only on technical feasibility but also on the incentives of firms that develop and deploy these systems. We show how profit maximization shapes safety investment in an AI supply chain with an upstream LLM provider and several competing downstream firms. In our game-theoretic model, we derive the market-driven level of safety investment and compare it with the levels that maximize market welfare and industry profit. We find that downstream competition generally induces downstream firms to invest more in safety than the industry-profit-optimal level. By contrast, the upstream provider may underinvest relative to these benchmarks because it is not fully compensated for the surplus from safety investments. Finally, we analyze how different regulatory interventions affect the participants' incentives and profits, and the resulting levels of model safety.

title: ClaimScope: Label-Blind Witness Verification for Mathematical Claim Auditing
abstract: Mathematical agents are commonly evaluated by answer accuracy or proof acceptance. We introduce ClaimScope, a 72-task benchmark for auditing proposed claims through a verdict, scope, counterexample, and repair. Tasks cover optimizer-state transport, finite-horizon affine recurrences, and exact $2\times2$ linear algebra. We evaluate Qwen3-8B with direct generation and four matched two-pass conditions, each starting from the same draft. A witness checker evaluates only the model's submitted state, without consulting reference verdicts or supplying a replacement witness. Its feedback still conveys information about validity: a verified refutation establishes that the claim is false, and rejection reasons can suggest structural fixes. In this evaluation, verifier feedback yields $23/39$ accepted counterexamples on invalid claims and $25/72$ safe completions, compared with $15/39$ and $20/72$ for checker-free generic feedback. Strict completion remains $17/72$; verdict accuracy changes from $47/72$ to $46/72$. The claim-grouped safe-completion difference is $.094$, with a bootstrap 95\% interval of $[.000,.198]$. All seven task-level gains follow horizon/input-length diagnostics. A post-hoc schema-only correction of the direct outputs reaches the same 25 safe tasks without another model call. These results separate claim classification from executable evidence, while locating the observed gains in witness-structure correction rather than demonstrating broader reasoning improvement.

title: BiShield-TEE: On the (In-)Security of Unilateral Weight Obfuscation in On-Device TEE-Shielded LLM Partition
abstract: On-device deployment of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly adopted due to latency and privacy requirements, but exposes proprietary models to reverse engineering and intellectual property theft. Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) provide hardware-enforced isolation for on-device inference, yet most TEE-based parameter obfuscation relies on unilateral matrix transformations that obfuscate only output side. We identify a vulnerability in this design, termed the \emph{Solution Determinacy Property (SDP)}: the obfuscation secret is uniquely determined, exposing the structure of the true key and enabling attackers to break the protection. Under our attacks, representative methods \textsc{GroupCover} and \textsc{ArrowCloak} are reduced to negligible protection, with attack accuracy reaching over $2.4\times$ the full-shielding black-box baseline and recovering near-complete model functionality.To address this vulnerability, we propose \textsc{BiShield-TEE}, a bilateral framework that induces \emph{Ambiguous Solutions} through joint obfuscation of input and output dimensions, hiding the true key among many equally valid candidates. Experiments across diverse models and datasets show that \textsc{BiShield-TEE} confines attack accuracy to the full-shielding black-box baseline, while achieving higher inference efficiency than prior methods on real hardware.Our code is available at https://github.com/laduiw/BiShield-TEE.

title: When Does Muon Actually Win? A Paired Data-, Time-, and Tuning-Budget Benchmark
abstract: Muon's gains in data efficiency motivate evaluating its performance under explicit data, time, and tuning budgets. On a single A100 GPU, we compare a reference single-device Muon implementation with AdamW across 17.7M- and 33.6M-parameter causal language models and 2.70M-parameter vision transformers. A common 23-candidate development budget selects configurations evaluated with five matched seeds, full validation trajectories, optimizer-step timing, and a frozen one-shot test. Muon reduces validation-loss area under the curve by 3.25--22.44\% at equal data and lowers test loss in all 20 primary pairs. In this configuration, Muon improves time-normalized loss area} by 19.68--22.31\% on vision, while AdamW is better by 3.38--6.96\% on language. The full Muon optimizer call, including auxiliary AdamW updates, consumes 56.1--69.6\% of training time, compared with 6.1--9.1\% for the AdamW baseline. Muon also has higher expected regret under restricted access to these candidate pools. These results characterize small models with reference kernels; their wall-clock ordering does not establish a ranking for larger models or optimized implementations.

title: Poison Valleys: Diagnosing Path-Dependent Failure in LLM Code Repair
abstract: When code-repair agents fail, final tests reveal that a patch is wrong but not which earlier commitment caused it or which software obligation failed. Poison Valleys traces this path in 1,844 model requests on two synthetic Python cases: PersistQueue adds atomic batch claiming to a disk-backed queue, while Dijkstra adds source-sensitive filtering to shortest-path search. We define plausible but incorrect software mechanisms, place each in a model's hypothesis, implementation plan, or both, and evaluate the generated code with an Oracle and targeted diagnostic coordinates. Moving the misconception from hypothesis to plan increased failure by 32.2% in PersistQueue and 28.9% in Dijkstra after matching the experimental mix. Different misconceptions produced distinct, model-dependent patterns of violated obligations, although several could converge on the same behavior. This creates a measured connection from upstream misconception to code mechanism and failure form. Code, data, and demo: https://poisonvalleys.org.

title: Does Compression Imply Generalization? A Minimum Description Length Perspective
abstract: A central question in modern learning theory is what notion of compression, if any, explains why over-parameterized neural networks generalize. Existing answers measure complexity at different levels, ranging from weights to representations; however, estimating the associated quantities either requires held-out data in principle or relies on the challenging (ultra) high-dimensional mutual information estimation. To overcome these challenges, we approach the question through the minimum description length (MDL) principle, and specifically, we propose the prequential regret as a complementary signal that is computable from the training trajectory alone. We establish that, in the (nearly) interpolating regime, the expected prequential regret upper-bounds the description length of the trained parameter under the algorithm-induced distribution, and that this description length translates into a high-probability generalization bound in the PAC-MDL setting. Along the way, we show that the encoder-complexity correction recently added to the algorithm-level information bottleneck (IB) is upper-bounded by an MDL parameter description length, \new{bringing together} the two views of compression from MDL and IB. Empirically, the prequential regret tracks the generalization error on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, with Pearson correlations exceeding 0.9.

title: Rethinking Learning from Label Proportions via Moment Matching
abstract: Learning from label proportions (LLP) is a weakly supervised setting where training data are grouped into bags with only bag-level label proportions observed, and the goal is to learn a classifier that predicts labels for individual instances. Recently, a large body of methods has emerged; however, most of them rely on the assumption that instance-label pairs are sampled i.i.d. and randomly assembled into bags, an assumption often violated in real-world scenarios. Our experimental results indicate that these methods perform suboptimally under non-random settings. In this work, we adopt a more realistic assumption: bags are sampled i.i.d., and instance labels are conditionally independent given the instances. Under this setting, we show that the label counts follow a Poisson multinomial distribution. Motivated by this observation, we propose LLP via moment matching (LLP-MM), a simple yet effective approach which leverages multi-order factorial moments as training objectives, encouraging the classifier predictions to match these moments and thereby more fully exploit the underlying statistical structure of the data. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets under various bag construction strategies demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach while maintaining high computational efficiency. Our code is available at https://github.com/TianhaoMa5/LLP-MM.

title: Fractional Power-of-Two Quantization for Efficient and Effective Multiplier-Free LLM Inference
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demand efficient inference, where the multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations in linear projections dominate compute and energy cost. Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces this cost by mapping weights and activations to low-bit integers. Power-of-Two (PoT) weight quantization promises efficient multiplier-free LLM inference via shift-add logic, but suffers significant accuracy degradation at low bitwidths due to its coarse base-2 quantization grid. We introduce Fractional PoT (FPoT), a base-$\sqrt{2}$ (half-octave) fractional PoT grid that achieves practical 4-bit weight quantization while preserving a fully integer shift-add datapath. The method combines (i) the base-$\sqrt{2}$ weight grid with uniform integer activations, (ii) a calibration-time grid-alignment refinement absorbed into the static per-channel scale, and (iii) a lightweight 1-adder $\sqrt{2}$ approximation whose error is absorbed during weight calibration via approximate-grid quantization, yielding a processing element (PE) with significantly fewer gates than a 4-bit integer multiplier.
